summary: A NASA-inspired astronaut health monitoring application featuring an interactive 3D anatomical human model, AI-powered ECG analysis, cardiovascular risk assessment, camera-based posture detection, facial wellbeing indicators, and real-time NASA space weather monitoring with offline data support.
details:
Project Description: NASA Astronaut Health Monitoring System

1. What does the project do and how does it work?

Our project is a NASA-inspired Astronaut Health Monitoring System designed to support astronaut health monitoring during space missions. It combines artificial intelligence, machine learning, interactive 3D anatomical visualization, and real-time space weather information in one application.

The application has three main AI diagnostic modules:

  • Module A – ECG Analysis: Uses a TensorFlow Lite machine learning model to analyze 187 ECG signal samples and classify heartbeat patterns into five categories: Normal, Supraventricular, Ventricular, Fusion, and Unknown.
  • Module B – Cardiovascular Risk Assessment: Uses a machine learning model that evaluates 12 health-related features, including age, gender, height, weight, blood pressure, cholesterol, glucose, and lifestyle factors to estimate cardiovascular risk.
  • Module C – Posture Analysis: Uses a camera and a TensorFlow Lite computer vision model to evaluate posture from a 224×224 image. It can also provide an angle-based estimate when a camera image is unavailable.

The application also includes an interactive 3D human anatomy viewer. Users can explore the human body, select anatomical regions, rotate and zoom the model, and independently display different anatomical systems, including skin, skeleton, muscles, and blood vessels.

Additionally, the application connects to NASA's DONKI Space Weather API to retrieve information about solar flares, energetic particle events, and geomagnetic storms. It refreshes the information periodically and stores the last successful results for offline access.

2. What benefits does the project have?

The main benefit is bringing multiple health-monitoring technologies together in one accessible platform.

It provides:

  • AI-assisted analysis of ECG signals and cardiovascular risk.
  • Camera-based posture assessment.
  • Interactive anatomical education through a 3D human model.
  • Space weather awareness through NASA data.
  • Offline access to previously retrieved space weather information.
  • A centralized dashboard for viewing health indicators and environmental conditions.

These features can help users understand the relationship between human physiology and the environmental challenges of space exploration.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Our primary goal is to contribute to the development of smarter and more accessible astronaut health-monitoring technologies.

During long-duration space missions, astronauts experience unique environmental conditions, including microgravity and increased exposure to space radiation. These conditions can affect cardiovascular health, muscles, bones, posture, and other physiological systems.

Our project demonstrates how machine learning and interactive visualization can help organize and interpret different types of health and environmental information.

In the future, the system could be expanded with real wearable sensor integration, continuous biometric monitoring, and more advanced predictive models. It is intended as a research and educational prototype rather than a certified medical diagnostic device.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software were used?

The project was developed primarily using:

  • Flutter: Main application framework and user interface development.
  • Dart: Primary programming language.
  • TensorFlow Lite / Flutter LiteRT: Running machine learning models directly on the device.
  • Dio: API communication and HTTP requests.
  • Perfectum 3D: Creating and displaying interactive 3D anatomical models.
  • Vector Math: 3D transformations, rotations, and spatial calculations.
  • Flutter Camera: Capturing images for posture analysis.
  • NASA DONKI API: Retrieving real-world space weather information.
  • JSON: Managing model parameters and cached environmental data.

Three machine learning models are integrated into the application: an ECG heartbeat classification model, a cardiovascular risk prediction model, and a posture assessment model.

The code also references the MIT-BIH heartbeat dataset and the cardiovascular disease dataset for the corresponding model modules.

The application is designed to run on compatible devices with camera support. No dedicated external medical hardware is required for the current software prototype.

5. How is the project creative and innovative?

The creativity of our project comes from combining technologies that are usually presented separately.

Instead of developing only a health application or only an anatomy visualization tool, we created a unified platform that connects human physiology with the space environment.

One of its most distinctive features is the interactive 3D anatomical viewer, which allows users to explore different body systems and select individual anatomical regions. The application also connects health indicators with a space mission environment, displaying how simulated environmental conditions and NASA space weather information can be considered alongside physiological data.

Another innovative aspect is running machine learning inference directly on the device, reducing dependence on external processing servers.

6. What factors did our team consider?

During development, our team considered several important factors:

  • Astronaut safety: The importance of monitoring physiological changes during long-duration missions.
  • Performance: Keeping machine learning inference and 3D visualization efficient.
  • Accessibility: Creating an understandable interface that brings complex information together.
  • Reliability: Supporting offline access to previously retrieved NASA data.
  • Modularity: Separating the application into independent diagnostic and visualization components.
  • Scientific relevance: Using established datasets and NASA's publicly accessible space weather information.
  • Future development: Designing a system that can eventually support additional sensors, more advanced AI models, and continuous monitoring.

Our overall objective is to demonstrate how artificial intelligence, computer vision, 3D visualization, and real-world space science data can work together to support the future of astronaut health monitoring.
